_strings.@@01cbc402f982: Credit for Income Tax Paid to Another State — Full-year residents or part-year residents of North Dakota who paid income tax to another state (or local jurisdiction in that state) on income also taxed by North Dakota.
_strings.@@0c1319d8acd5: Marriage Penalty Credit — Married couples filing a JOINT North Dakota return where both spouses have qualified income (wages/salaries/tips from Form 1040 line 1z, net self-employment income, and taxable retirement/Social Security amounts). Qualifies only if joint ND taxable income (Form ND-1 line 18) exceeds $78,836 AND the lower-earning spouse's qualified income exceeds $46,275 (2024 indexed amounts — up from $74,862/$43,980 in 2023). Designed to offset the higher tax that two-earner couples pay versus filing as singles.

_strings.@@46c0cd2c2f5a: If any of your income was exempt from federal tax under a treaty: ND does not conform to federal tax treaties, so that income is still taxable to ND — do not carry the federal exclusion onto the state return.
_strings.@@4784802f4f12: Renter's Refund (Renter's Property Tax Refund / circuit-breaker) — A North Dakota renter who is age 65 or older OR has a permanent and total disability (physician's certificate or SSA/agency determination required), whose income (including spouse and dependents) does not exceed $70,000 for the calendar year preceding the assessment date. Rent must be for the renter's place of residence or a mobile home lot (heat, water, lights, telephone, and furniture costs do not count as rent; properties exempt from property tax, such as nursing homes, do not qualify). There is no asset limitation for renters.

_strings.@@556a0e90de78: Treaty conformity — ND does NOT conform to federal tax treaties: income exempt from federal tax under a treaty is STILL taxable by ND. Do not carry a federal treaty exclusion onto the state return. (This is about TREATY conformity only — a state's Internal Revenue Code conformity date and its deduction/credit conformity are separate questions; see any law-change lines below.) State note: ND does NOT conform — it re-taxes federally treaty-exempt income. Although the ND-1 resident return starts from federal taxable income (Form 1040/1040-SR line 15, ND-1 line 1b), the 2024 ND-1 Individual Income Tax Booklet (p.5) states: "Except where an income tax treaty between the United States and a foreign country specifically exempts income from taxation by a U.S. state, income tax treaties between the U.S. and foreign countries do not apply for North Dakota income tax purposes. Therefore, you may have to pay North Dakota income tax on gross income from North Dakota sources even though the income is exempt from U.S. income tax because of a treaty." The mechanism is in the Guideline: Income Taxation of Nonresident Aliens — the taxpayer must complete a Pro Forma U.S. Form 1040NR but "you must disregard any instruction to the U.S. income tax return that refers to the treaty," then carry that pro-forma 1040NR line 15 (with treaty income NOT excluded) to ND-1 line 1b. So treaty-exempt income that drops out of the actual federal return is effectively added back (rebuilt) before flowing into ND income. This is the same non-conforming posture as CA/CT/MD/MS. The treaty pass-through applies ONLY where a treaty article specifically extends the exemption to the 50 U.S. states.

_strings.@@a5e4656a3756: Homestead Property Tax Credit — A North Dakota homeowner who is age 65 or older OR has a permanent and total disability (no age requirement for disability; proof required), who lives at and has an ownership interest in the property (co-ownership prorates the credit), and whose income (including spouse and dependents) does not exceed $70,000 for the calendar year preceding the assessment date. state_tax.work_common_tail: . Tax line: Form ND-1 (2024), page 2, line 20: 'Tax - If full-year resident, enter tax on amount on line 19 from Tax Table in instructions. If full-year nonresident or part-year resident, enter tax from Schedule ND-1NR, line 23. All filers: If you have farm income or sold a research credit, see instructions.' Line 19 is the North Dakota taxable income carried from line 18 (= line 1b federal taxable income + additions lines 2-4a - subtractions). This op computes the state's rate-schedule tax line ONLY — county/city add-on taxes, state credits, and any amounts outside the rate schedule are NOT modeled. Pack notes: Base guidance: Supply federal taxable income — Form 1040/1040-SR line 15, which is entered on Form ND-1 line 1b. If any North Dakota additions (ND-1 lines 2-4a, e.g. the planned gift/endowment credit adjustment) or subtractions (lines 5-17, e.g. U.S.-obligation interest, net long-term capital gain exclusion, qualified dividend exclusion, Social Security exclusion) apply, supply Form ND-1 line 19 (North Dakota taxable income, carried from line 18 = line 1b + additions - subtractions, floored at 0) instead. The brackets apply directly to that figure with nothing further subtracted: North Dakota has no state standard deduction and no personal/dependent exemptions — the federal standard/itemized deduction is already embedded in federal taxable income. Nonresident-alien edge case: ND does not conform to federal treaty exemptions; an NRA must build a Pro Forma 1040NR disregarding treaty provisions and use its line 15 as ND-1 line 1b. 2024 RE-INDEXATION (structure unchanged from the 2023 reform): the three-bracket 0% / 1.95% / 2.5% system continues with inflation-adjusted boundaries — single 0% band now to $47,150 (2023: $44,725) and the 2.5% bracket now starting at $238,200 (2023: $225,975); MFJ/QSS $78,775 / $289,975 (2023: $74,750 / $275,100); MFS $39,375 / $144,975 (2023: $37,375 / $137,550); HoH $63,175 / $264,100 (2023: $59,950 / $250,550). The rates themselves are unchanged. The shipped schedules are the ones printed in the 2024 booklet (p.28). Tax Table mandate below $100,000: the booklet's 'Line 20 - Tax' instructs full-year residents to use the Tax Table (pp.20-27, $50 income bands), and the rate-schedule page itself says to use the schedules only 'If your North Dakota taxable income is $100,000 or more.' Table values are the schedules evaluated at the band midpoint (verified: single $50,100-$50,150 row prints $58 = 1.95% x ($50,125 - $47,150) = $58.01 rounded), so bracket math may differ from the table by about a dollar within a band; the filed form must use the table below $100,000. Qualifying surviving spouse (Form ND-1 filing status 5) uses the Married filing jointly column — the 2024 rate schedule is titled 'Married filing jointly and Qualifying surviving spouse' and the Tax Table is footnoted '*If a Qualifying surviving spouse, use the Married filing jointly column'; the engine's QSS-to-MFJ mapping is exactly correct. Printed '$X + Y% of amount over $Z' top-bracket constants reconcile with cumulative bracket sums to within half a cent: Single $3,725.48 printed vs exact 1.95% x $191,050 = $3,725.475 (+$0.005); MFJ/QSS $4,118.40 = 1.95% x $211,200 exactly; MFS $2,059.20 = 1.95% x $105,600 exactly; HoH $3,918.04 printed vs exact 1.95% x $200,925 = $3,918.0375 (+$0.0025). Pure marginal bracket math (what this op does) therefore matches the printed schedules to the cent after whole-dollar rounding. No state standard deduction and no personal or dependent exemptions: ND starts from federal taxable income (Form 1040 line 15 -> ND-1 line 1b), which already reflects the FEDERAL standard or itemized deduction; nothing further is subtracted before the rates apply. Pass exemptions_count=0 and dependents_count=0. ND additions and subtractions (ND-1 lines 2-17: e.g. 40% net long-term capital gain exclusion, qualified dividend exclusion, Social Security benefit exclusion, U.S.-obligation interest, ND-1SA items) are NOT modeled — if any apply, compute ND-1 line 18/19 on the form and supply that as the base. Marriage penalty credit (Form ND-1 line 22, maximum $303 for 2024, up from $287) is a nonrefundable CREDIT subtracted from tax for joint filers where joint ND taxable income exceeds $78,836 and the lower-earning spouse's qualified income exceeds $46,275 — computed on the booklet worksheet (p.14, $14,600 line-5 constant); it is NOT an income exemption and is not modeled by this op. The line 21 credit for income tax paid to another state (Schedule ND-1CR) and line 23 Schedule ND-1TC credits are likewise not modeled. Full-year nonresidents and part-year residents do not use this computation directly: their tax comes from Schedule ND-1NR line 23 (the full-year tax prorated by the ND income ratio); this pack reproduces the full-year-resident tax on ND-1 line 20 only. Alternate computations not modeled: farm income averaging via Schedule ND-1FA (federal Schedule J filers) and tax on proceeds from the sale of a research expense credit via Schedule ND-1CS — ND-1 line 20 directs those filers to the instructions. ND does NOT conform to federal income tax treaties (booklet p.5): treaty-exempt income is effectively rebuilt into the base via a Pro Forma 1040NR that disregards treaty provisions, whose line 15 becomes ND-1 line 1b. No mid-year 2024 rate change: the three-bracket system enacted effective tax year 2023 (0%/1.95%/2.5%) simply carried into 2024 with indexed boundaries; the 2024 booklet prints one set of schedules for the whole year.
